video_title: The Biggest Losers of the Year | Animal Spirits 490
gist: Animal Spirits hosts Michael and Ben review a chaotic 2026: Nvidia down ~35% after Jensen Huang's resignation over a scandal tied to alleged chip shipments to China, while the S&P 500 index investor ends up the year's winner (up ~9% YTD, max drawdown ~9%). They debate whether Nvidia's founder-centric structure makes it a GE/IBM-style fallen giant, flag a record semis price/forward-earnings divergence, sticky tariff/energy inflation with an 85%-odds December Fed hike, a simultaneous crash in gold, silver, Bitcoin and Ethereum, and a frozen housing market.

insights.claim: One co-host argues the market is underreacting to Jensen's resignation from Nvidia: with the stock down ~35% from highs (S&P 500 only ~5% off highs), he expects it to fall further and believes the company's best days are behind it.
insights.speaker: Animal Spirits co-host
insights.so_what: Contrarian bear call on the market's dominant AI name; watch whether NVDA drifts toward a 50% drawdown rather than recovering.
insights.quote: I think the market is wrong here. I think Nvidia is toast.

insights.claim: The bull counter on Nvidia: it remains the dominant AI player with ~70% gross margins, a software operating system moat beyond hardware, locked-in contracts, and trades at only ~11 times forward earnings.
insights.speaker: Animal Spirits co-host
insights.so_what: At ~11x forward with 70% gross margins, the valuation already discounts a lot; key debate is whether earnings themselves are now impaired.

insights.claim: Ben Thompson's framing: Nvidia's most important moat was that it was organized as an 'exoskeleton' around Jensen himself (about 60 direct reports, little management, no succession plan), so his departure leaves the structure more prone to collapse than investors expect.
insights.speaker: Ben Thompson (cited by hosts)
insights.so_what: Founder-dependence risk: companies run as startups around one person carry key-man risk that multiples may not capture.
insights.quote: Wong organized Nvidia as an exco exoskeleton around one man himself.

insights.claim: The Wall Street Journal reported records showing the company of the former Nvidia CEO's one-time mistress arranged to send nearly $12 billion of top-of-the-line Nvidia chips (several hundred thousand units) to companies in China, the chips US export controls aimed to block.
insights.speaker: Animal Spirits co-host (citing WSJ)
insights.so_what: Export-control violations raise regulatory, congressional and legal overhang for Nvidia and the chip sector; expect a prolonged, choppy process.
insights.quote: arranged to send nearly $12 billion worth of topofthe-line Nvidia chips to companies in China

insights.claim: Nvidia went from a ~$50 billion company ten years ago and ~$150 billion at end-2019 to nearly $6 trillion, rising from 1% of the S&P 500 in December 2022 to 8.5% by May 2026.
insights.speaker: Animal Spirits co-host
insights.so_what: Shows the scale of index concentration risk tied to one stock and one executive.

insights.claim: Citing Michael Cembalest's work on fallen index giants (GM, IBM, GE, Exxon), a co-host now thinks Nvidia is the most likely of the mega-caps to become a former-largest company that languishes as a shrinking index weight, a view he says he would not have held 10 days earlier.
insights.speaker: Animal Spirits co-host
insights.so_what: Mega-cap leadership can end abruptly; consider the historical pattern of former index leaders underperforming for years.

insights.claim: Unlike Zuckerberg, Dell, Ellison, Musk or the Google founders, Jensen held about 3% of Nvidia's equity with no dual-class control, which made his ouster possible; founder-controlled companies (Zuckerberg controls ~60% of Meta's vote) carry concentrated scandal risk.
insights.speaker: Animal Spirits co-host
insights.so_what: Governance structure determines whether boards can act on a scandal; dual-class mega-caps carry a different key-man risk.

insights.claim: Wall Street Journal reporting suggested Nvidia was already pulling back from being the 'bank of AI' with an open checkbook before the scandal, which tightens funding for the AI ecosystem.
insights.speaker: Animal Spirits co-host (citing WSJ)
insights.so_what: Less vendor financing from Nvidia hurts neoclouds and AI startups that relied on it.

insights.claim: A co-host raises the risk that government involvement ends tech-company independence, which he sees as a large market risk; the other co-host says it would not make his top-10 risk list.
insights.speaker: Animal Spirits co-hosts
insights.so_what: Watch for congressional or regulatory intervention in mega-cap tech after the Nvidia affair.

insights.claim: The S&P 500 semiconductors index shows a record divergence: stock prices are crashing while forward earnings keep rising, a gap not seen even around 2008; one host thinks it will prove a severe overreaction because hyperscaler demand is not slowing.
insights.speaker: Animal Spirits co-host
insights.so_what: If AI makes chip earnings less cyclical, the price/earnings gap could close upward; a potential setup for semis bulls.

insights.claim: SMH (VanEck semiconductor ETF) is down ~30% from its highs and DRAM is down ~50%, yet they are still up 41% and 28% respectively for the year; South Korea and Taiwan country ETFs are in 30-40% drawdowns while still the year's best performers.
insights.speaker: Animal Spirits co-host
insights.so_what: Drawdowns are large relative to gains; momentum-heavy regions and semis remain exposed.

insights.claim: Hosts say the election results (meaning fewer data centers will likely be built) plus the Nvidia scandal gave investors a reason to sell AI stocks, and investors were already rejecting heavy free-cash-flow burn at Meta, Google and Oracle.
insights.speaker: Animal Spirits co-hosts
insights.so_what: Capex-heavy hyperscalers face a market that penalizes FCF burn; watch capex guidance.

insights.claim: Levered long ETF AUM is down 37%, compared with 44% in the tariff drawdown, 54% in the 2022 bear market and 30% in the March Iran episode, which hosts read as a significant leverage washout.
insights.speaker: Animal Spirits co-host (citing Todd Sohn, Strategas)
insights.so_what: Leverage flushes often mark late-stage selling; a contrarian signal.

insights.claim: Retail aggressively bought the Nvidia dip: Vanda Research recorded the biggest-ever opening-30-minute retail net buying in Nvidia ($111 million, 40x normal), and Nvidia took 61% of US retail net buying Monday-Wednesday.
insights.speaker: Animal Spirits co-host (citing Vanda Research)
insights.so_what: The buy-the-dip reflex is intact; extreme retail concentration can extend volatility.
insights.quote: Jensen's resignation sparked the biggest ever opening 30 minutes of retail net buying we've recorded in Nvidia.

insights.claim: A Wall Street Journal piece cites a value investor saying the AI trade makes up ~40% of all hedge fund portfolios, and hosts argue AI-automated and agentic investing will make herding and leveraged swings even worse.
insights.speaker: Animal Spirits co-hosts
insights.so_what: Crowding plus AI-driven herding raises the risk of sharp, correlated unwinds.

insights.claim: One co-host's possible upside case: the Nvidia shock could slow AI spending, give overheated AI stocks a needed breather, and end bubble talk, which would be good for the long term even if it hurts in the short run.
insights.speaker: Animal Spirits co-host
insights.so_what: A slower AI buildout could favor FCF-positive companies over capex-heavy spenders.

insights.claim: Anthropic is set to IPO the same week and the offering is oversubscribed despite the AI selloff.
insights.speaker: Animal Spirits co-host
insights.so_what: A test of private-to-public AI appetite during a sector drawdown.

insights.claim: Tech trades at ~17x forward earnings versus ~24x for consumer staples; one host says the flight to defensives is rotation (money must go somewhere), not a valuation call, and staples are only ~5% of the index.
insights.speaker: Animal Spirits co-hosts
insights.so_what: Staples' premium multiple reflects flows and may reverse if tech stabilizes.

insights.claim: The S&P 500 index investor is the hosts' 'winner' of 2026: the index is up ~9% year to date with a max drawdown of only ~9% (in March), and it gained 2.5% in the week Nvidia fell almost 15%.
insights.speaker: Animal Spirits co-host
insights.so_what: Diversification absorbed the single-stock shock; supports a passive core holding.

insights.claim: Through the first ten months, the Russell 1000 Value was up almost 25% while Russell 1000 Growth was roughly flat, and both US and international small-cap value are outperforming the S&P 500.
insights.speaker: Animal Spirits co-host
insights.so_what: A real factor rotation toward value; hosts note some AI winners such as Micron grew earnings enough to migrate into value indexes.

insights.claim: The hosts' 2026 losers list includes Netflix (down ~45% YTD), Oracle (down ~60%), Bitcoin (down ~33%), software, private credit, Nike and first-time homebuyers.
insights.speaker: Animal Spirits co-hosts
insights.so_what: Lists the year's sharpest losers for tax-loss harvesting and mean-reversion screens.

insights.claim: The weighted share of CPI components rising faster than 2% annualized has jumped to 76%, the highest since August 2022, and markets price about 85% odds of a 25bp Fed hike in December.
insights.speaker: Animal Spirits co-host
insights.so_what: Rate-hike risk is back; position for higher front-end yields.
insights.quote: The odds of a 25 basis point rate hike in December is 85%.

insights.claim: Goldman Sachs estimates almost the entire US inflation overshoot can be explained by tariffs and the war in Iran, and this energy/tariff inflation is not producing wage gains, so inflation is outpacing wages again.
insights.speaker: Animal Spirits co-host (citing Goldman Sachs)
insights.so_what: Supply-driven inflation hurts real incomes and consumer sentiment without wage support.

insights.claim: One co-host argues only a recession will bring inflation meaningfully lower (ending the war or tariffs aside), framing the choice as a recession or ~3% inflation.
insights.speaker: Animal Spirits co-host
insights.so_what: Raises recession odds as the Fed tightens into supply-driven inflation.
insights.quote: The thing that no one wants to admit though, the only way we're going to slow inflation and bring it down is a recession.

insights.claim: A record 45% of Americans expect their financial situation to be worse a year from now, and the labor share of income has resumed its long decline after a short pandemic spike, which hosts link to the midterm swing despite decent macro data.
insights.speaker: Animal Spirits co-hosts
insights.so_what: Political volatility driven by inflation anger can shift policy on tariffs, housing and tech.

themes.theme: Hard assets crash on real rates

insights.claim: Bitcoin, Ethereum, gold and silver are crashing at the same time: gold down ~30% from highs, silver ~60%, Ethereum ~60%, Bitcoin ~50%, which a host attributes to rising real interest rates and flows reversing.
insights.speaker: Animal Spirits co-hosts
insights.so_what: Store-of-value assets trade as one real-rate and flow trade; higher real yields are the main headwind.

insights.claim: Hosts note how quickly the spring narratives of de-dollarization, dollar decline and deficit fear faded, and say the dollar is fine.
insights.speaker: Animal Spirits co-hosts
insights.so_what: Narrative-driven debasement trades unwind fast when real rates rise.

insights.claim: Existing home sales are at their lowest level since the GFC, the 30-year mortgage rate has passed 7.5%, and home prices have been roughly flat (about 1% growth) for two years.
insights.speaker: Animal Spirits co-hosts
insights.so_what: Housing turnover stays frozen; homebuilders and transaction-driven businesses face headwinds.

insights.claim: A host proposes tax breaks and fast-tracked permitting for homes of 1,500 sq ft or less, citing data that the median new single-family home is ~2,100 sq ft versus 983 sq ft in 1940.
insights.speaker: Animal Spirits co-host
insights.so_what: Starter-home policy would favor builders focused on smaller entry-level product.
